{{Short description|Theorem in Lie theory in mathematics}}
In [[Lie theory]], an area of [[mathematics]], the '''Kazhdan–Margulis theorem''' is a statement asserting that a [[discrete subgroup]] in [[semisimple Lie group]]s cannot be too dense in the group. More precisely, in any such [[Lie group]] there is a uniform [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of the [[identity element]] such that every lattice in the group has a [[Conjugacy class#Conjugacy of subgroups and general subsets|conjugate]] whose intersection with this neighbourhood contains only the identity. This result was proven in the 1960s by [[David Kazhdan]] and [[Grigory Margulis]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kazhdan | first1=David | author1-link=David Kazhdan | last2=Margulis | first2=Grigory | author2-link=Grigory Margulis | title=A proof of Selberg's hypothesis | journal= [[Mathematics of the USSR - Sbornik|Math. USSR Sbornik]] | volume=4 | pages=147–152 | date=1968 | doi=10.1070/SM1968v004n01ABEH002782 | lang=en|mr=0223487 | translator= Z. Skalsky | url = https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1070/SM1968v004n01ABEH002782/pdf| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Statement and remarks ==

The formal statement of the Kazhdan–Margulis theorem is as follows.

:''Let <math>G</matH> be a semisimple Lie group: there exists an open neighbourhood <math>U</math> of the identity <math>e</math> in <math>G</math> such that for any discrete subgroup <math>\Gamma \subset G</math> there is an element <math>g \in G</math> satisfying <math>g\Gamma g^{-1} \cap U = \{ e \}</math>. ''

Note that in general Lie groups this statement is far from being true; in particular, in a [[Nilpotent group|nilpotent]] Lie group, for any neighbourhood of the identity there exists a lattice in the group which is generated by its intersection with the neighbourhood: for example, in <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, the lattice <math>\varepsilon \mathbb Z^n</math> satisfies this property for <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> small enough.

=== Proof ===

The main technical result of Kazhdan–Margulis, which is interesting in its own right and from which the better-known statement above follows immediately, is the following.{{sfn|Raghunathan|1972|loc=Theorem 11.7}}

:''Given a semisimple Lie group without compact factors <math>G</math> endowed with a norm <math>|\cdot|</math>, there exists <math>c > 1</math>, a neighbourhood <math>U_0</math> of <math>e</math> in <math>G</math>, a compact subset <math>E \subset G</math> such that, for any discrete subgroup <math>\Gamma \subset G</math> there exists a <math>g \in E</math> such that <math>|g\gamma g^{-1}| \ge c|\gamma|</math> for all <math>\gamma \in \Gamma \cap U_0</math>. ''

The neighbourhood <math>U_0</math> is obtained as a [[Zassenhaus neighbourhood]] of the identity in <math>G</math>: the theorem then follows by standard Lie-theoretic arguments.

There also exist other proofs. There is one proof which is more geometric in nature and which can give more information,<ref>{{cite journal

== Applications ==

=== Selberg's hypothesis ===

One of the motivations of Kazhdan–Margulis was to prove the following statement, known at the time as ''Selberg's hypothesis'' (recall that a [[Lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattice]] is called ''uniform'' if its quotient space is compact):

:''A lattice in a semisimple Lie group is non-uniform if and only if it contains a [[unipotent]] element. ''

This result follows from the more technical version of the Kazhdan–Margulis theorem and the fact that only unipotent elements can be conjugated arbitrarily close (for a given element) to the identity.

=== Volumes of locally symmetric spaces ===

A corollary of the theorem is that the [[locally symmetric space]]s and orbifolds associated to lattices in a semisimple Lie group cannot have arbitrarily small volume (given a normalisation for the Haar measure).

For hyperbolic surfaces this is due to Siegel, and there is an explicit lower bound of <math>\pi / 21</math> for the smallest covolume of a quotient of the [[hyperbolic plane]] by a lattice in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)</math> (see [[Hurwitz's automorphisms theorem]]). For hyperbolic three-manifolds the lattice of minimal volume is known and its covolume is about 0.0390.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Marshall | first1=Timothy H. | last2=Martin | first2=Gaven J. | title=Minimal co-volume hyperbolic lattices, II: Simple torsion in a Kleinian group | journal= Annals of Mathematics | volume=176 | date=2012 | pages=261–301 | mr=2925384 | doi=10.4007/annals.2012.176.1.4| doi-access=free }}</ref> In higher dimensions the problem of finding the lattice of minimal volume is still open, though it has been solved when restricting to the subclass of [[arithmetic group]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Belolipetsky | first1=Mikhail | last2=Emery | first2=Vincent | title=Hyperbolic manifolds of small volume | journal=[[Documenta Mathematica]] | volume=19 | date=2014 | pages=801–814 | doi=10.4171/dm/464 | doi-access=free | arxiv=1310.2270 | s2cid=303659 | url=https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/documenta/vol-19/26.pdf}}</ref>

=== Wang's finiteness theorem ===

Together with [[local rigidity]] and finite generation of lattices the Kazhdan-Margulis theorem is an important ingredient in the proof of Wang's finiteness theorem.<ref>Theorem 8.1 in {{Citation
| last  = Wang
| first = Hsien-Chung
| author-link = Hsien Chung Wang
| chapter = Topics on totally discontinuous groups
| date = 1972
| editor-last1  = Boothby  
| editor-first1 = William M.
| editor-last2  = Weiss
| editor-first2 = Guido L.
| title  = Symmetric Spaces, short Courses presented at Washington Univ.
| volume = 1
| publisher = Marcel Dekker
| series = Pure and Applied Mathematics. 
| number = 8
| pages = 459–487
| publication-date = 1972
| isbn = 
| zbl = 0232.22018
}}</ref>

:''If <math>G</matH> is a simple Lie group not locally isomorphic to <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)</math> or <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C)</math> with a fixed Haar measure and <math>v>0</math> there are only finitely many lattices in <math>G</math> of covolume less than <math>v</math>. ''
